extracted.intended_audience: writers, researchers, communicators, and press/marketing professionals using APA style and seeking bias-free, inclusive language
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing bias-free, respectful, and precise language across identities (race, ethnicity, disability, gender, age, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, etc.) for professional communications and publications, including press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use people-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to people as people first (e.g., 'person with schizophrenia' rather than 'a schizophrenic'), unless a community explicitly prefers identity-first language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Person-first phrasing emphasizes the person before the condition. Anti-pattern: using diagnostic labels as nouns ('the autistic') unless preferred by the group. Note exceptions exist (some communities, e.g., many autistic people, prefer identity-first language). When in doubt, ask or follow community preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor identity-first preferences when specified
rubrics_metrics.description: If a group or individual prefers identity-first language (e.g., 'autistic person'), use that preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check current community guidance and individual preference. When reporting research, make explicit whether speakers prefer identity-first wording. Avoid assuming universal preference across a group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stigmatizing labels and pejorative terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use words that imply moral failing, pathology, or shame (e.g., 'addict,' 'abuse' as character labels, 'crazy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral, descriptive phrases ('person with a substance use disorder' rather than 'addict'). Avoid clichés and slang that demean groups. Replace moralizing verbs (e.g., 'suffers from') with neutral verbs (e.g., 'has' or 'diagnosed with').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific, accurate terms for race and ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise names (e.g., 'Navajo Nation,' 'Mexican,' 'Dominican') instead of broad or vague labels when possible; recognize the difference between race and ethnicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specific nation/ethnic identity is known and relevant, name it. Avoid using nationality as a proxy for race. When referring to groups collectively, use the term the group uses for itself. Be cautious with umbrella terms ('people of color')—use only when appropriate and with explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization conventions for racial and ethnic group names
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow capitalization guidelines for group names (e.g., capitalizing 'Black' and 'Indigenous' as proper nouns when recommended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the current style guidance in the manual (e.g., capitalize racial and ethnic group names as proper nouns where advised). Be consistent throughout the document. If guidance changes, adopt the most current authoritative recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid outdated, offensive, or clinical terms for sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use current, accepted terms (e.g., 'gay,' 'lesbian,' 'bisexual,' 'queer' when appropriate) and avoid clinical or pejorative terms like 'homosexual' or 'sexual preference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer language that communities use for themselves. Avoid implying orientation is a choice. Use ‘sexual orientation’ rather than ambiguous phrasing and avoid pathologizing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect gender identity and pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the names and pronouns that individuals use; use gender-neutral language when gender is unknown or irrelevant; use singular 'they' when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and use pronouns in contexts that normalize sharing (e.g., bios). Reword sentences to avoid gendered markers when unnecessary (e.g., 'chair' instead of 'chairman'). Do not assume pronouns based on appearance or name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusive terminology for family and relationship structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use neutral words (e.g., 'partner,' 'spouse,' 'caregiver,' 'parent') rather than heteronormative or traditional assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming a binary or traditional family structure; specify roles rather than gendered terms when relevant. When referring to legal relationships, be precise ('married partner' if legally married).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary mention of identity characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Only mention race, ethnicity, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or other identity characteristics when they are relevant to the content or analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevant mention can otherize or stigmatize. If identity is relevant, explain why and provide context. Anti-pattern: gratuitous descriptors in headlines or leads that do not pertain to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nonableist phrasing and accurate disability language
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe disabilities in neutral, accurate terms (e.g., 'person who uses a wheelchair' or 'person with a mobility impairment'), avoiding language that implies suffering or confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases like 'confined to a wheelchair,' 'wheelchair-bound,' or 'suffering from' disability. Prefer 'uses a wheelchair' or 'has [condition]' unless the community prefers otherwise. When describing accessibility features, use clear, factual language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid euphemisms and sensational metaphors for illness, disability, or demographic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use metaphors that equate groups with disease, crime, or natural disasters, or euphemisms that obscure meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language like 'plague of immigrants' or 'curb the spread of [group].' Use precise, non-metaphorical language when discussing groups or conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, neutral language for mental health
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to mental health conditions in clinical, person-first, nonjudgmental terms (e.g., 'person with major depressive disorder' or 'people experiencing depression').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stigmatizing constructions like 'mentally ill person' as a primary identifier or 'committed suicide' (prefer 'died by suicide'). Provide context for prevalence and avoid sensationalizing descriptions of behavior related to mental health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use respectful, nonpejorative language about substance use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use medical, nonjudgmental terms (e.g., 'person with a substance use disorder'; avoid 'addict' or 'abuser').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid criminalizing or moralizing language; when reporting legal matters, separate behavior from identity and avoid conflating use with criminality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use age-appropriate, nonstigmatizing language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid antiquated or derogatory terms ('the elderly'); prefer 'older adults' or specific age ranges when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume abilities or preferences based on age. Use neutral descriptors and only note age when relevant; specify numeric ranges if needed for clarity in research or reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using 'minority' as a blanket descriptor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use more specific descriptors for groups (e.g., 'racial minority groups' or name the groups) rather than the vague term 'minority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When demographic composition is referenced, consider whether 'minority' accurately reflects numbers or power dynamics; use precise, contextual wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe socioeconomic status with precision and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use neutral phrases like 'people experiencing poverty' or 'low-income communities' rather than labels such as 'the poor' or 'underclass.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying moral failure or criminality related to economic status. When reporting statistics, define metrics (e.g., federal poverty level) and contextualize structural causes when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate terminology for nationality, citizenship, and immigration status
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'immigrant,' 'migrant,' 'undocumented person,' 'citizen,' and nationality; avoid using nationality as shorthand for ethnicity or race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'illegal' to describe people; instead use 'undocumented' or the legally precise term. Be careful with labels like 'alien'—they are dehumanizing in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusive occupational and role language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer neutral job titles (e.g., 'firefighter,' 'server,' 'police officer') and avoid gendered or stereotyped role descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing ability or competence, focus on credentials and actions rather than identity. Avoid diminutive or infantilizing descriptors for roles performed by women, older adults, or marginalized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow people to self-identify and report preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, ask individuals how they identify and what terms/pronouns they prefer, and honor those preferences in writing and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In surveys or interviews, provide options and open-text fields for self-description. In publication, respect stated preferences and clarify when reporting that preferences varied or were not collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reporting research, define and justify identity measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, disability, and other identities were measured, categorized, and why those categories were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report who collected the data and whether participants self-identified. Describe limitations of categories and how they may affect interpretation. Avoid treating demographic variables as interchangeable or explanatory without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent, precise, and current
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terminology consistently within a document and keep up to date with evolving, community-led terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the latest edition guidance and community statements. Where terminology is evolving or contested, explain the chosen terms and rationale. Update style in subsequent editions or releases when norms change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid binary-only framing when not appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume binary categories for sex, gender, or other characteristics when a spectrum or multiple categories are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide options beyond male/female in forms and reporting when relevant (and ensure ethical considerations). Use gender-inclusive language ('people,' 'they') in general descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mindful use of descriptors in headlines and leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid leading with an identity descriptor (race, religion, disability) in headlines or leads unless it is integral to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight identity only when directly relevant. Anti-pattern: emphasizing identity to sensationalize or otherize (e.g., 'Black man arrested' when race is unrelated to the incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphors and idioms that demean groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from using idioms that are rooted in ableism, racism, sexism, or other biases (e.g., 'turn a blind eye,' 'suffers a breakdown' in stigmatizing contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with literal, clear language. Be mindful that metaphors can perpetuate stigma even when not intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trauma-informed, non-sensational language for violence and harm
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting violence, sexual assault, or trauma, use language that avoids victim-blaming and sensational detail; prioritize survivors' dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'survivor' or 'person who experienced [act]' over labels that reduce the person to the event. Avoid lurid detail and explain context and supports available when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, consult communities and authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: If uncertain about appropriate terminology, consult community organizations, style guidance updates, and subject-matter experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document consultation and preference when possible. Acknowledge contested terms and explain chosen usage in editorial notes or methodology sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating descriptive statistics with normative judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Present demographic or health statistics without implying inferiority, causation, or moral valuation of groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize disparities by discussing structural, historical, and systemic contributors rather than implying individual blame.
